function: Beam hopping pattern for LEO satellites: multi-agent DRL decides which beam positions each satellite illuminates per time slot, maximizing throughput and minimizing delay fairness (p. 6).
system: Forward link, 2 LEO satellites at 500 km, M=8 beams over 35 beam positions, Ku-band 12 GHz, 500 MHz, full frequency reuse; no RIS (pp. 3-4, 8).
method: Multi-agent reinforcement learning: one dueling double DQN (D3QN, CNN) per satellite with value decomposition (VDN); centralized training, distributed execution; reward from throughput and delay fairness (pp. 5-8).
data_channel: Own simulator: Friis free-space loss, lognormal rain fading, ITU-R S.1528 antenna pattern, Poisson traffic 50-300 Mbps per beam position; no external dataset (pp. 4, 8).
test_conditions: Trained 2000 episodes of 200 slots at 50-300 Mbps, weight beta swept; tested in the same 2-satellite setup, traffic up to 350 Mbps (pp. 8-12).
baselines: Non-learned: random, periodic, throughput-greedy, delay-greedy, rank-based beam hopping, genetic algorithm [31]. Learned: only VDN-DDQN, VDN-DQN, and fully-connected variants of the proposed framework (p. 9).
metrics: System throughput (bps) and delay fairness (ms, max-min delay gap) versus episode, weight and traffic demand; per-beam throughput and delay; loss (pp. 5, 10-13).
complexity: Order of complexity of the CNN per decision, O(sum M_l^2 N_l^2 C_{l-1} C_l), and orders of the heuristic baselines; no runtime or FLOPs (pp. 9-10).
q1_support: p. 4: "the LEO satellite channel mainly includes free space loss, atmospheric attenuation and beam gain". Missing: no 3GPP TR 38.811 channel or measured data; the paper builds its own link budget, with ITU-R S.1528 used only for the antenna pattern (p. 4).
q2_support: p. 8: "In training stage, the maximum arrival rate of beam positions is 300 Mbps and the minimum arrival rate is 50 Mbps." Missing: no other constellation, number of satellites or beams, or traffic model is tested; the traffic sweeps (p. 12) reach 350 Mbps but are presented as load sweeps in the same setup.
q3_support: p. 9: "The VDN-DDQN framework replaces D3QN with DDQN in the proposed VDN-D3QN framework." The VDN-DQN and fully-connected baselines are defined the same way, so they are variants; the other six baselines (random, periodic, greedy, rank-based, genetic algorithm) are non-learned, and no earlier learned beam-hopping method is compared.
q4_support: p. 9: "we analyze the computational complexity of proposed algorithms in each time slot", given as the order O(sum M_l^2 N_l^2 C_{l-1} C_l) of the convolutional network, with the orders of the baselines on pp. 9-10.
q5_support: p. 8: "Table II summarizes the simulation parameters." Missing: the channel and traffic are simulated by the authors, and no code or data link and no public dataset appear in the 14 pages.
notes: Included, area 6: beam hopping is learned beam control for satellite links, which Step 1 rule 4 treats as physical layer. q1 = 0 is a judgement: the channel is the authors' own link budget (Friis loss from a textbook [27], lognormal rain fading with fixed mu and sigma, ITU-R S.1528 pattern; p. 4), and the sentence naming an "ITU-R rainfall attenuation model" cites [28], which is S.1528 (p. 14); the reviewer may treat ITU-R as another standardized model. q2 = 0: training traffic is 50-300 Mbps (p. 8) and the sweeps of Figs. 16-18 reach 350 Mbps (p. 12), but they are load sweeps in the same 2-satellite setup. q3 = 0: the learned baselines are variants of the proposed framework by the paper's own definition (p. 9); it would flip to 1 if the reviewer counts VDN-DQN and VDN-DDQN as standard algorithms on the same problem. The text for Fig. 15 says 50-300 Mbps while its axis reaches 350 (p. 12). Table II and the figures were read from the page images.
